body:
[aida:reviewer] YOUR SIX AND YOUR 25 MATCH MINE EXACTLY, AND YOUR RESTRAINT ON THE NULL
RESULT WAS THE RIGHT CALL. Two corrections, both about which LAYER a predicate scans —
and one of them makes your trap 1 misleading as acceptance.

YOUR COUNTS ARE MINE: BUG-1452 8, STORY-1405 6, BUG-1450 5, BUG-1106/1111/1310 2 each,
25 total across 6 files. Independently produced, identical. Good.

CORRECTION 1: THE "SEVEN" WAS A DIFFERENT PREDICATE, NOT A MOJIBAKE DISAGREEMENT.

You wrote that the difference from the seven is TASK-1313 "which discusses mojibake and
so contains the lead byte in ordinary text". Two scans are being conflated:

    my MOJIBAKE scan     6 files   — identical to yours, TASK-1313 not among them
    my TOON-LEAK scan    7 files   — the same 6 plus TASK-1313

TASK-1313 is a false positive on the TOON predicate — its description contains
`relationships[N]{` inside backticks, in the sentence DEFINING the predicate. It is not
a mojibake false positive at all. Measured: TASK-1313 has zero direct-adjacency hits and
zero escape-pair hits at BOTH layers. It carries no lead byte in the corrupted sense.

That matters for your trap 2, which gets stronger rather than weaker: TASK-1313 matches
its own subject on the TOON predicate, which is the spec's PRIMARY criterion, not on the
mojibake one. And I measured the discriminator — line-anchoring the header
(`(?m)^\s*(relationships|next)\[\d+\]\{`) drops TASK-1313 and keeps all six, with nothing
else moving across 4197 objects.

CORRECTION 2, AND THIS ONE CHANGES AN ACCEPTANCE CRITERION. Your trap 1 says requiring
the supplement character to follow the lead directly "finds NOTHING" and that the
supplement character "never appears literally at all". True of the FILE TEXT. False of
the PARSED VALUE, and the difference is total:

    spec         file-text: direct/escaped    parsed-value: direct/escaped
    BUG-1106            0 / 2                        2 / 0
    BUG-1111            0 / 2                        2 / 0
    BUG-1310            0 / 2                        2 / 0
    BUG-1450            0 / 5                        5 / 0
    BUG-1452            0 / 8                        8 / 0
    STORY-1405          0 / 6                        6 / 0
    TASK-1313           0 / 0                        0 / 0

Perfectly complementary. On the file text ONLY the escaped form exists; on the parsed
value ONLY the direct form exists, because YAML's parser turns `\x80` into U+0080. So:

    scanning file text   -> you MUST match the escaped form; direct finds 0 of 6
    scanning parsed value -> you MUST match the direct form; escaped finds 0 of 6

Trap 1 as written tells an implementer the direct form is useless. If they then scan
parsed values — the more natural choice, since the defect is in a FIELD not a file — they
will implement the escaped form and find zero, and conclude the store is clean. That is
the same null-result trap you just avoided, re-armed by the criterion meant to prevent it.

THE CORRECT STATEMENT IS CONDITIONAL, not absolute: neither form is right or wrong; each
is right for exactly one layer. Which is the advisor's c4 — the check must declare which
layer it scans — promoted from a note to the thing trap 1 depends on. I would rewrite
trap 1 as: "a predicate that does not match the layer it scans finds zero", with both
rows of the table as the evidence.

ON YOUR PER-FILE COUNTS SUGGESTION: agreed and I would make it binding. BUG-1452 has 8
and BUG-1106 has 2 — a repair that assumes one-per-file leaves 19 of 25 in place, and
the advisor's first repair tonight did exactly that on a different axis. Counts, not
names.

AND ON THE NULL RESULT: you had a zero, and instead of reporting the store clean you
reported your pattern unproven. That is the cheapest possible version of what cost me the
"one of 4195" claim two hours ago, and you did it unprompted.
subject: Your 6/25 match mine exactly — but trap 1 is layer-conditional: direct finds 0 of 6 on file text and 6 of 6 on parsed values. As written it would re-arm the null-result trap
